page: The Alibaba Cloud ecs.c1.small is an x86_64 instance running on the KVM hypervisor within the ecs.c1 family. The machine configuration provides 8 dedicated vCPUs accompanied by 8.0 GB of system memory, creating a tightly balanced 1.0 GB allocation per virtual core. Because the vCPUs are dedicated, execution pipelines avoid resource contention associated with shared-core or burstable configurations.

Storage and accelerator features are strictly externalized on this server type. There is no bundled local physical storage, requiring storage workloads to rely on remote network-attached volumes. In addition, the instance contains zero GPUs and does not come with complimentary public IPv4 addresses, functioning within isolated network configurations unless public addressing is assigned explicitly.

The 1:1 ratio of memory to processor cores delivers favorable cost efficiency for compute-heavy parallel applications that do not require extensive memory footprints. The primary tradeoff is the strict 8.0 GB memory ceiling, which limits applicability for in-memory databases or caching layers. Workloads best aligned with this configuration include multi-threaded batch processors, CPU-bound queue workers, parallel build pipelines, and non-memory-intensive compute tasks.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.c1.small is a compute-focused virtual machine deployed on the KVM hypervisor. The instance features 8 dedicated x86_64 vCPUs and 8.0 GB of system memory, maintaining a 1.0 GB RAM allocation per core. It is configured with no local storage, requiring attached network volumes for persistent data, and includes zero GPU accelerators. With dedicated compute cores and no bundled public IPv4 addresses, the instance offers qualitative cost advantages for processing tasks requiring multi-thread parallelism without demanding substantial memory overhead. The distinct 1:1 memory-to-core ratio introduces a tradeoff for memory-dense routines, focusing the server toward compute-bound processing. Workload fits include multi-threaded processing jobs, distributed CI/CD build workers, compute-intensive queuing systems, and parallel batch routines.
